subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look up at the sky tonight. If it is clear over Mogadishu, Hargeisa, or the beaches near Mombasa, you will see a huge dark blanket sprinkled with tiny lights, and often a bright, glowing Moon. Have you ever wondered why the Moon is sometimes a thin curved sliver, like the tip of a fingernail, and sometimes a full round circle as bright as a lamp? Have you wondered why the Sun comes up in the morning and goes down at night, so that we have day and then darkness? In this unit you are going to become a real sky scientist, called an astronomer, and you will learn the answers.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, if you study carefully and try the activities, you will be able to do all of these things. Read them now, and read them again at the end to see how much you have grown.
Describe Earth, the Sun, and the Moon as spherical (ball-shaped) objects, not flat.
Compare the sizes of Earth, the Sun, and the Moon, and say which is biggest and which is smallest.
Explain that Earth spins on its axis and that this spinning causes day and night.
Explain that Earth orbits the Sun once each year.
Describe how the Moon orbits Earth about once every month.
Name and put in order the main phases of the Moon, from new Moon to full Moon and back.
Explain why the Moon appears to change shape, using the idea of sunlight and shadow.
Record your own careful observations of the Moon over several nights, like a real scientist.
Use science words such as orbit, rotate, phase, sphere, crescent, and gravity correctly.

concepts.title: Everything in the Sky is Round Like a Ball
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin with a big idea. Earth, the Sun, and the Moon are all shaped like balls. We call this shape spherical, which just means round like a football or an orange. Long ago, before people had cameras and rockets, some thought Earth was flat like a giant plate. But clever observers noticed clues that showed Earth is really a giant ball, and today we have photographs taken from space that show Earth as a beautiful blue and white sphere floating in the dark.

How can we tell that Earth is round without flying into space? Here is one clue you could see for yourself on the coast. Imagine you are standing on the beach at Berbera or Kismaayo, watching a big ship sail away toward the horizon. As the ship goes far away, it does not simply get smaller and smaller until it is a dot. Instead, the bottom of the ship disappears first, then the middle, and the very top disappears last. It is as if the ship is sinking down behind a hill of water. That gentle hill is the curve of the round Earth. If Earth were flat, the whole ship would stay in view and just shrink to a tiny speck.

There are more clues. When you climb up high, to the top of a tall hill in the Rift Valley, you can see much farther than when you stand on flat ground, because you are looking over the curve of the Earth. Travellers long ago noticed that the patterns of stars change when you journey far to the north or far to the south, which would not happen on a flat world. And during a special event called a lunar eclipse, when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, you can watch Earth's shadow fall on the Moon, and that shadow is always curved and round, because Earth is round.

Think about a football lying on the ground. From wherever you stand around it, it always looks round. A flat plate is different: from the side it looks like a thin line, and only from above does it look round. Earth behaves like the football, not the plate. No matter where an astronaut floats in space, Earth always looks like a full round ball, blue with oceans and swirled with white clouds. That is one of the clearest signs that our planet is a true sphere. It is a wonderful thought that the same ground you walk on, from the beaches of the Indian Ocean to the highlands of the Rift Valley, is all part of one enormous gentle curve.
concepts.example: The Sun and the Moon are round too. The Sun is a gigantic ball of glowing, burning gas, so hot and bright that you must never, ever look straight at it because it can hurt your eyes badly. The Moon is a ball of rock and dust with no air and no water. When you look at a full Moon, notice how it is a perfect circle, the same way a ball looks like a circle when you draw around it. That roundness is your own eyes telling you the Moon is a sphere.

concepts.title: Big, Bigger, Biggest: Sizes in Space
concepts.explanation:
Now let us think about size. Which is biggest: Earth, the Sun, or the Moon? Many children guess wrongly, because in the sky the Sun and the Moon look almost the same size, like two small coins held up high. But that is a trick of distance. The truth is that the Sun is by far the biggest, then Earth is in the middle, and the Moon is the smallest of the three.

Here is a way to picture it using things from around your home. Imagine the Moon is a small marble, or a single date. Then Earth would be about the size of an orange, quite a bit bigger. But the Sun would be enormous, wider than a whole house or a mosque! If the Sun were a big beach ball, Earth would be smaller than a peppercorn beside it. The Sun only looks small in the sky because it is so, so far away, far beyond anything you can walk or drive to.

So why do the Sun and the Moon look about the same size when we look up? It is a wonderful coincidence. The Sun is huge but extremely far away. The Moon is tiny but very close to us. The bigness of the Sun and its great distance balance out with the smallness of the Moon and its closeness, so from Earth they appear roughly the same size. Think of it this way: a giraffe standing far across the savanna can look the same height as your thumb held close to your eye. Distance changes how big things seem.
concepts.example: ⭐ Did You Know? The Sun is so wide that if it were hollow, more than one million Earths could fit inside it. And yet the Sun is only a medium-sized star. There are stars far bigger, so far away that they look like tiny sparkles at night.

concepts.title: Why We Have Day and Night
concepts.explanation:
Every single day the Sun seems to rise in the east, climb across the sky, and set in the west. It looks as if the Sun is moving around us. But here is the surprising truth: the Sun is not travelling around Earth each day. Instead, Earth is spinning. This spinning is called rotation.

Picture Earth as a giant ball turning slowly around an imaginary line that runs through its middle from top to bottom. That imaginary line is called the axis. Earth turns around this axis like a spinning top or like a globe you push with your finger. It takes 24 hours — one whole day and night — for Earth to spin around one complete time.

Now think about the Sun shining on this spinning ball. The Sun can only light up the half of Earth that is facing toward it. On that half it is bright: that is day. The other half of Earth is turned away, into its own shadow, so it is dark there: that is night. As Earth keeps spinning, your part of the world is slowly carried from the dark side into the light, and morning comes. Hours later your part turns away again, and evening falls into night. Day and night are simply your home being carried into and out of the sunlight as Earth turns.

This is why, when it is bright midday in Mogadishu, it is the middle of the dark night on the opposite side of the world, in places far across the ocean. They are on the shadow side while you are on the sunny side. It also explains why the Sun appears to rise in the east: because Earth spins toward the east, the Sun peeks over the eastern horizon first each morning, over the Indian Ocean, and sinks in the west behind the land in the evening.
concepts.example: There is a second movement too. As well as spinning around its axis each day, Earth is also travelling in a great big circle around the Sun. This journey is called an orbit, and it takes a whole year — about 365 days — for Earth to go all the way around the Sun once. So Earth is doing two things at the same time: spinning like a top (which gives us day and night) and swinging around the Sun in a giant loop (which gives us a year). Both movements happen smoothly and quietly, and gravity keeps everything in its proper path.

concepts.title: The Moon, Earth's Faithful Companion
concepts.explanation:
The Moon is Earth's closest neighbour in space and its natural companion. While Earth orbits the Sun, the Moon orbits Earth. It takes the Moon about one month — roughly 29 or 30 days — to travel all the way around Earth one time. As it circles us, it keeps us company through every night.

Here is something surprising and important: the Moon does not make its own light. The Moon has no fire and no glow of its own. It is a ball of grey rock. The reason the Moon shines so brightly at night is that the Sun's light bounces off it, like sunlight bouncing off a shiny wall or off the surface of the sea. Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun, just like half of Earth is always lit. The Moon is like a mirror in the sky, catching the Sun's light and sending some of it down to us so that our nights are not completely black.

Another gentle wonder: we always see the same face of the Moon. The Moon turns in such a perfect way as it orbits that the same side is always pointing toward Earth. So the patterns of light and dark you see on the Moon — the shapes some people call the face of the Moon — are the same shapes your grandparents and their grandparents saw. The other side of the Moon, which always points away from us, was a mystery until spacecraft flew around and took photographs of it.
concepts.example: 🌙 Did You Know? The Moon is held close to Earth by gravity, the same invisible pull that makes a dropped stone fall to the ground. Gravity is like an unbreakable, invisible rope between Earth and the Moon. Without it, the Moon would drift away into space, and our nights would lose their beautiful lamp.

concepts.title: The Phases of the Moon
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to one of the most beautiful patterns in the whole sky: the phases of the Moon. If you watch the Moon night after night for a month, you will see it slowly change shape. First there is no Moon at all, or only a whisker-thin curve. Then a thin crescent appears. Night by night the bright part grows fatter, until half the Moon is lit, then almost all of it, until at last a glorious round full Moon shines. Then it shrinks back again, night by night, until it disappears, and the whole story begins once more. This complete cycle, from one new Moon to the next, is called a lunar month.

Why does this happen? Remember that the Sun always lights up exactly half of the Moon. The Moon is not really changing its shape — it is always a whole ball. What changes is how much of the lit half we can see from Earth, and that depends on where the Moon is on its journey around us. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces away from us and we see its dark side: that is the new Moon, and it is almost invisible. When the Moon is on the far side, opposite the Sun, we see its whole lit half shining back at us: that is the full Moon. In between these, we see slices — crescents and half-Moons — depending on the angle.

Here are the main phases in order, so you can follow the story: new Moon (dark and hidden), then a thin waxing crescent (a growing sliver), then the first quarter (half lit), then a fat gibbous shape, then the bright full Moon, then it shrinks through a fading gibbous, the last quarter (the other half lit), a thin waning crescent, and back to new Moon. The word waxing means growing bigger, and waning means shrinking smaller. The whole cycle takes about 29 to 30 days — almost exactly one month.

Here is a helpful way to remember which way the crescent curves. When the Moon is waxing (growing) in the evening, the bright curved edge points toward where the Sun has just set, in the west. Little by little each night the lit part grows fatter and the Moon appears higher in the sky and stays up longer. When the Moon is waning (shrinking) after the full Moon, it rises later and later, often not appearing until deep in the night or the early morning. If you keep your own Moon diary over several nights, you will begin to feel this rhythm for yourself, and you will be able to guess what shape the Moon will be tomorrow. That is exactly how real astronomers, and how families watching for the Ramadan crescent, learn to read the sky.

The phases of the Moon matter deeply in the lives of Muslim families. The Islamic calendar, the Hijri calendar, is a lunar calendar, which means each month follows the Moon. A new month begins when the thin new crescent Moon is first sighted in the evening sky. This is why the beginning of Ramadan, the blessed month of fasting, is announced when people look for and see the new crescent. And the end of Ramadan, the joyful festival of Eid al-Fitr, also begins with the sighting of the next new crescent. When you learn to read the Moon's phases, you are learning to read a calendar that your family and your community have followed for many, many centuries. Each lunar month is about 29 or 30 days, which is why the Islamic year is a little shorter than the ordinary school-year calendar, and why Ramadan moves to a slightly earlier time each year.
concepts.example: 🌊 Did You Know? Because the Moon reflects the Sun's light, moonlight is really sunlight that has travelled a long way and bounced off the Moon to reach you. On a clear night by the Indian Ocean, the path of shimmering silver light across the water is sunlight that has bounced off the Moon and then off the waves before reaching your eyes.

concepts.title: The Moon, the Tides, and the Ocean
concepts.explanation:
The Moon does not only give us light. Its gravity — that same invisible pull — reaches all the way to Earth and gently tugs on our oceans. This pull helps create the tides, which are the slow rising and falling of the sea along the coast. If you have visited the shore at Mombasa, Lamu, or Dar es Salaam, you may have noticed that sometimes the water comes far up the beach (high tide) and other times it pulls back and leaves wide wet sand and rock pools (low tide). This gentle in-and-out breathing of the sea happens because the Moon's gravity pulls the ocean water toward it as the Moon travels around Earth.

Fishermen along the East African coast have always understood the tides, even before they knew the Moon was the cause. They know when the water will be high enough to sail out and when it will be low enough to gather shellfish among the rocks. The tides are a daily reminder that the Moon, so far away, still reaches down and touches our lives here on Earth.

methods.title: Making Day and Night With a Ball and a Torch
methods.example: To model how Earth's spinning causes day and night, and to see why one side is light while the other is dark.
steps: Stick the sticker on one spot of the ball. This spot is your home town, such as Mogadishu.
Make the room dark. Ask a helper to hold the torch still and shine it at the ball from one side. The torch is the Sun.
Notice that only the half of the ball facing the torch is lit. The other half is in shadow.
Turn the ball slowly around, keeping the torch still. Watch your sticker move from the lit side into the shadow and back again.
Say "day" out loud when your sticker is in the light, and "night" when it is in the shadow.

methods.title: Modelling the Phases of the Moon
methods.example: To see for yourself why the Moon appears to change shape, and to make the phases of the Moon with a ball and a torch.
steps: Darken the room. Place the torch on a table so it shines steadily across the room. This is the Sun.
Hold the ball out at arm's length. Your head is Earth, and the ball is the Moon.
Turn so the ball is directly between your face and the torch. Look at the side of the ball facing you — it is dark. This is the new Moon.
Turn slowly to your left, keeping the ball up. Watch a thin curved sliver of light appear on the ball. This is the crescent.
Keep turning. When the torch is to your side, half the ball you see is lit. This is the first quarter.

methods.title: Your Own Moon-Watching Diary
methods.example: To observe the real Moon over many nights, like a true astronomer, and to discover the pattern of its phases with your own eyes.
steps: Choose a time each evening when you can see the Moon, at roughly the same time each night. Always go with an adult.
Each clear night, look at the Moon and carefully draw its shape in your notebook.
Write down the date and the time next to your drawing.
Note where the Moon is in the sky — low near the horizon, or high up.
Do this for as many nights as you can over two to four weeks. On cloudy nights, simply write "cloudy — no Moon seen."

methods.title: How Far, How Big? A Size Model of Earth and Moon
methods.example: To compare the sizes of Earth and the Moon using objects from your kitchen, and to understand that Earth is much bigger than the Moon.
steps: Place the orange on the table. This is your Earth.
Beside it, place a date stone, a marble, and a chickpea in a row.
The real Moon is about one quarter as wide as Earth. Look at your Earth-orange and choose the object that looks about one quarter as wide.
Hold your chosen Moon next to the Earth-orange and compare them.
Now place your Moon-object about one metre (a big step) away from the orange to show that the Moon is far from Earth, not touching it.

workedExamples.title: Counting the Days of the Lunar Month
workedExamples.prompt: Astronomers and families use the Moon to count time, so let us practise a little counting together, step by step.
workedExamples.solution:
Question: The new crescent Moon is sighted, marking the first day of the month. About how many days later will the Moon be full and round? And about how many days after that will it return to a new Moon again?

Step 1 — Remember the whole cycle. One complete lunar month, from new Moon to the next new Moon, takes about 29 to 30 days. Let us use 30 days to keep our counting simple.

Step 2 — Find the full Moon. The full Moon happens about halfway through the cycle, because that is when the Moon has travelled halfway around Earth. Half of 30 is 15. So the full Moon comes about 15 days after the new crescent.

Step 3 — Return to new Moon. After the full Moon, the Moon shrinks back over the second half of the cycle. That is another 15 days. So 15 days plus 15 days equals 30 days — one full lunar month — and the new crescent appears once more.

workedExamples.prompt: What shape are the Earth, the Sun, and the Moon? (a) flat like a plate (b) square like a box (c) spherical like a ball (d) triangular
workedExamples.solution: 1 c — spherical All three are round balls, not flat. Photos from space and everyday observation show this.

activities.title: Making Day and Night With a Ball and a Torch
activities.materials: A round ball, an orange, or a grapefruit (this is your Earth); A torch, or a phone light, or a lamp (this is your Sun); A small sticker, or a spot drawn with a marker (this is your town); A darkened room
steps: Stick the sticker on one spot of the ball. This spot is your home town, such as Mogadishu.
Make the room dark. Ask a helper to hold the torch still and shine it at the ball from one side. The torch is the Sun.
Notice that only the half of the ball facing the torch is lit. The other half is in shadow.
Turn the ball slowly around, keeping the torch still. Watch your sticker move from the lit side into the shadow and back again.
Say "day" out loud when your sticker is in the light, and "night" when it is in the shadow.

activities.title: Modelling the Phases of the Moon
activities.materials: A small ball, an orange, or a ball of foil (this is the Moon); A bright torch or lamp (this is the Sun); A darkened room; Your own head in the middle (this is the Earth — you are standing on Earth!)
steps: Darken the room. Place the torch on a table so it shines steadily across the room. This is the Sun.
Hold the ball out at arm's length. Your head is Earth, and the ball is the Moon.
Turn so the ball is directly between your face and the torch. Look at the side of the ball facing you — it is dark. This is the new Moon.
Turn slowly to your left, keeping the ball up. Watch a thin curved sliver of light appear on the ball. This is the crescent.
Keep turning. When the torch is to your side, half the ball you see is lit. This is the first quarter.

activities.title: Your Own Moon-Watching Diary
activities.materials: A notebook or some sheets of paper; A pencil; A calendar to note the dates; A grown-up to watch the sky with you
steps: Choose a time each evening when you can see the Moon, at roughly the same time each night. Always go with an adult.
Each clear night, look at the Moon and carefully draw its shape in your notebook.
Write down the date and the time next to your drawing.
Note where the Moon is in the sky — low near the horizon, or high up.
Do this for as many nights as you can over two to four weeks. On cloudy nights, simply write "cloudy — no Moon seen."

activities.title: How Far, How Big? A Size Model of Earth and Moon
activities.materials: One orange or a medium ball (this is Earth); One small item such as a date stone, a marble, a chickpea, or a small pebble (choices for the Moon); A ruler or tape measure (optional); A table to lay them on
steps: Place the orange on the table. This is your Earth.
Beside it, place a date stone, a marble, and a chickpea in a row.
The real Moon is about one quarter as wide as Earth. Look at your Earth-orange and choose the object that looks about one quarter as wide.
Hold your chosen Moon next to the Earth-orange and compare them.
Now place your Moon-object about one metre (a big step) away from the orange to show that the Moon is far from Earth, not touching it.
Safety: Small objects must never go in your mouth, nose or ears. Keep them away from babies and toddlers.

activities.title: Observe: The Phases of the Moon
activities.materials: A round ball, an orange, or a grapefruit (this is your Earth); A torch, or a phone light, or a lamp (this is your Sun); A small sticker, or a spot drawn with a marker (this is your town); A darkened room
steps: Look for an example of the phases of the moon around your home or outside.

connections.text: Gravity, the pulling force you met before, is what holds the Moon near Earth and keeps us on the ground.
The Moon shines by reflecting light, and day and night are about light and shadow on a spinning Earth.
The lunar calendar, the Ramadan and Eid crescent, and reflecting on the order of creation all connect to this unit.
Understanding the Earth as a sphere, the oceans, and the tides links science to the world map.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, if you study carefully and try the activities, you will be able to do all of these things. Read them now, and read them again at the end to see how much you have grown.
I can describe Earth, the Sun, and the Moon as spherical (ball-shaped) objects, not flat.
I can compare the sizes of Earth, the Sun, and the Moon, and say which is biggest and which is smallest.
I can explain that Earth spins on its axis and that this spinning causes day and night.
I can explain that Earth orbits the Sun once each year.
I can describe how the Moon orbits Earth about once every month.
I can name and put in order the main phases of the Moon, from new Moon to full Moon and back.
I can explain why the Moon appears to change shape, using the idea of sunlight and shadow.
